body.text: There are just three days until polling day in Victoria, with political parties ramping up their campaigns around the state in a last-minute bid to sway undecided voters.
Follow our live coverage below:
Submit a comment or question
Live updates
Jess Wilson cleans up graffiti in Prahan
Liberal leader Jess Wilson is painting over graffiti in the seat of Prahran this morning, illustrating her pitch to Victorian voters that she will "clean up Victoria".
Wilson is promising $5 million to establish a Clean Up Crew if elected, which would involve a rapid response team to remove graffiti, mow lawns and clean up rubbish.
Victorians would be able to nominate a local "eyesore" for the team to clean up.
Today's graffiti clean-up is just the latest in a year of stunts Wilson has used to take aim at the Labor government.
Earlier this year, she and a team of MPs mowed lawns on a median strip along Victoria Parade to attack the government on its maintenance record.
"I'm a can-do person, let's just get it done," Wilson said.

Pakenham voters weigh in
State political reporter Richard Willingham had a chat to some Pakenham voters in line.
Vijay, who runs a food kiosk at Pakenham Marketplace, says life is increasingly difficult as a small business owner and he is looking for a change.
"The government should look after small businesses, the tax going on, the CGT everything, it's killing us," he says."At the moment we're struggling."
"The government should look after small businesses, the tax going on, the CGT everything, it's killing us," he says.
"At the moment we're struggling."
For Toni, who recently started a family, the cost-of-living crisis is at the front of mind this election.
"It's feeling like the financial part of our state is collapsing," she says.
Toni says she is voting Liberal, and believes Labor has spent "way too much" on things Victorians don't need.
And One Nation are at least guaranteed one vote, with longtime supporter Hank turning up to volunteer.
Hank says he was one of the first members of the party in Victoria, joining 28 years ago.
And he has glowing reviews for leader and candidate Warren Pickering.
"He's the man for the job. I like his background," Hank says."Down to earth, practical, wasn't born with a silver spoon, he did it tough and he did it the hard way and he'll be here for a long time."
"He's the man for the job. I like his background," Hank says.
"Down to earth, practical, wasn't born with a silver spoon, he did it tough and he did it the hard way and he'll be here for a long time."
Pakenham Liberal candidate says people 'ready for a change'
Also on hand in Pakenham at the early voting centre was Liberal candidate Radmila Dyson.
A relative newcomer to politics, Dyson is reported to have been a Liberal Party member for less than a year before her preselection and required special dispensation to run.
She told our state political reporter Richard Willingham she has doorknocked more than 4,000 houses in the electorate, and says people are ready for a new government.
"I'm feeling great, the vibe is excitement, everyone's really ready for a change," she says.
The seat of Pakenham is extremely marginal, with retiring Labor MP Emma Vulin winning the seat by a margin of just 0.4 per cent.
Now, the seat faces fresh competition from One Nation, which Dyson admits is a challenge.
"I'm not overly confident with everything, but I'm confident that people in Pakenham know that … [Jess] has got the team and the policies in place to actually make a difference," she says.
In contrast to what we saw earlier today in Mill Park, Dyson says the Pakenham race has been very calm and friendly.
"Everyone has been really kind, regardless of what side of politics, people in Pakenham are beautiful," she says.
Pickering admits candidate's Dezi Freeman support 'not helpful'
The ABC's Richard Willingham raised with Pickering the topic of One Nation's vetting processes for candidates.
It comes after media reports that One Nation's Williamstown candidate Catherine Loughnan made social media posts comparing police killer Dezi Freeman to Ned Kelly and calling Victoria Police corrupt.
Pickering admits the comments were "absolutely not helpful".
But he says the major parties have also dealt with similar issues.
"We don't have the 50, 80 years infrastructure of the major parties. However, they have that in place and they're still enduring the same sorts of problems," he says.
The Liberal Party was forced to dump its own Williamstown candidate Paul Lindemann after it was revealed he made racist social media posts.
Warren Pickering talks to the ABC in Pakenham
The ABC's state political reporter Richard Willingham is in Pakenham today, where One Nation leader Warren Pickering is hoping to win the seat.
Pickering was at an early voting centre at the Pakenham Scout Group this morning, talking to voters waiting in line.
He was upfront with voters who did not want to take a One Nation how-to-vote card.
"I keep reminding people you don't need to be polite, we've got pretty thick skin … you can tell us to bugger off," he said.
Pickering stopped to chat with Willingham about his party's vision for Victoria's future.
He said one "non-negotiable" for the party was providing transparency around scandals such as COVID, hotel quarantine, the Commonwealth Games and the Big Build.
"Transparency of the cabinet papers that we believe Victorians need to see, to show Victorians how we got here in the first place," he says.
Pickering denied One Nation had the backing of billionaires, saying the party was a grassroots movement.
"Contrary to a lot of the rhetoric of this party somehow having billions of dollars, we absolutely do not, we're all volunteers," he says.
Seats in focus: Prahran
Prahran has changed hands many times over its long history, being one of the most consistently marginal seats in the state.
Although it has somewhat settled as a progressive-leaning seat in the 21st century, it has still been represented by all three of Labor, the Liberals and the Greens.

The seat first became a genuine three-party contest in 2014. At that election the Greens grew their primary vote by five percentage points and were able to overtake Labor into second place, using their preferences to narrowly win the seat from the Liberals.
The successful Greens candidate, Sam Hibbins, held the seat with increasingly healthy margins at the following two elections, eventually reaching first place on the primary vote in 2022.
He resigned in late 2024 after admitting to having an affair with one of his staff.

Labor opted not to run in the ensuing by-election and the Liberal Party narrowly regained the seat from the Greens. This was partially due to low turnout and unfavourable preference recommendations from other candidates including former Labor MP for the seat Tony Lupton, who was running as an independent.
With Labor returning to the contest, the Greens will be hoping to regain Prahran in 2026.
Racist graffiti left at voting centre in Melbourne's west
Party campaigners arrived to an ugly scene at an early voting centre for the seat of Werribee today.
The words "No" and "Black" appear to have been spraypainted overnight onto the side of the 1st Iramoo Scout Hall in Wyndham Vale.
Corflutes for several candidates were also defaced.
Labor MP John Lister says he's contacted the Victorian Electoral Commission (VEC) about the graffiti.
"Our community will not stand for this kind of racist attack. I call on all political parties to condemn this behaviour," Lister says.
The VEC doesn't comment on individual matters but said every Victorian had the right to participate in the election safely and free from intimidation or interference.
"Reported damage to property, including election signage or corflutes for a state election is a matter for Victoria Police," the VEC spokesperson said.
We've also contacted Victoria Police and the Victorian Greens for comment.
Liberal leader rules out gas exploration subsidies
Opposition Leader Jess Wilson says subsidies and tax breaks are not on the table under her plan to open up the state to more gas exploration and extraction.
A key plank of the Coalition's energy plans is for more gas to be used, despite dwindling supplies and the cost of finding new gas.
Experts are also warning that new gas will take at least five years to bring to market; Victoria's energy crunch is in just two years' time.
Speaking to the ABC's Richard Willingham on her election campaign bus, Wilson says she wants to make it easier for more gas extraction.

Wilson: "I've said I want to see expressions of interest on my desk."Willingham: "So is that subsidies and tax breaks?"Wilson: "That's not on the table; what we are talking about is speeding up that process, how do we make sure it's a process that is driving industry to go after gas?"

Key Event
🎞️:Ben Carroll confronted by One Nation volunteer
For the second time in as many days, the premier has been confronted by a One Nation volunteer, during a fiery campaign visit in Melbourne's north.
Carroll has been pounding the pavement in Bundoora this morning alongside Labor candidate Elizabeth Nealy, who is looking to succeed retiring MP Lily D'Ambrosio.
After Carroll arrived at an early voting centre, he was shouted at by a One Nation volunteer as he spoke with reporters.
In a wide-ranging tirade, the volunteer called Labor a "demonic" party, and called for a royal commission into the COVID-19 vaccines as she held a crucifix towards Carroll.
Carroll for the most part ignored the woman, simply stating that everyone was entitled to their say.
The ABC's Leanne Wong said the volunteer kept up her aggressive rant for several minutes, before the premier was escorted away by security.
Doctors release final election scorecard
The Australian Medical Association has published its final ratings of the major parties over their health commitments.
AMA Victoria says Labor, the Coalition, the Greens and One Nation all responded to the 10 priorities put to them.
AMA Victoria's president, Simon Judkins, says there has been some encouraging developments during the campaign, as far as doctors are concerned.
"Less than a year ago, the government announced that VicHealth would be absorbed into the Department of Health.
"We now have commitments from the Coalition, the Greens and One Nation to retain its independence.

"We have welcomed substantial commitments to hospital care, planned surgery, specialist appointments and patient travel assistance, as well as Labor's commitment to plan a 100-bed acute mental health unit at Casey Hospital following advocacy by AMA Victoria."

Seats in focus: Polwarth

Polwarth has been held by conservative parties for more than 100 years, including the Liberal Party, which has won the seat at every election it contested since its creation. It has had just three members since 1985, all of whom have served on the Liberal front bench.
Current MP Richard Riordan won the seat in a 2015 by-election to succeed former roads and public transport minister Terry Mulder.

Riordan has been a significant figure in the party's conservative wing and served on the opposition front bench from September 2021 until Jess Wilson's elevation to the Liberal leadership in November 2025.
He was a particularly strong supporter of former leader Brad Battin, backing him for the leadership in 2022 after suspending his own leadership bid.
Under Riordan, Polwarth has become significantly more marginal and he goes into this election with a two-party preferred margin of just under 2 per cent.
Labor is running the same candidate as 2022 but its statewide position will make winning the seat difficult.
It could be that the Liberals are more under threat from One Nation due to the seat's older and less culturally diverse demographics.
Your guide to the minor parties in the 2026 state election
We focus a lot on the four parties that are polling to claim the vast majority of votes come election day.
But there are of course many additional parties running in the 2026 Victorian election, each with their own vision for the state's future.
If you want to learn more, we've got you covered from A(ffordable Housing Now) to V(ictorian Socialists) in our guide below:
Voting numbers pass 1.5 million
The Victorian Electoral Commission says that, as of this morning, 1.5 million Victorians have cast their vote in the state election.
That includes people who've visited early polling centres, overseas and interstate voting locatons, or people who've voted by phone or post.

"We have already seen a high number of Victorians actively participate in their democracy," Electoral Commissioner Sven Bluemmel says."There is a voting option for everyone, so find the best option for you, and make sure you cast your vote before 6pm on election day, Saturday, 28 November."

"There is a voting option for everyone, so find the best option for you, and make sure you cast your vote before 6pm on election day, Saturday, 28 November."
If you're planning to vote by post in this election, you have until 6pm to get your application in.
Ben stops by a bakery
Ben Carroll's tour on Melbourne's north continues, as he makes a stop at a Lebanese bakery in Campbellfield, after spruiking Labor's free dental policy in Broadmeadows.
Political parties exempt from privacy laws

I received a letter from the liberals addressed to me directly over the weekend. There's no chance I've signed up for any communication from them — surely this is a breach of confidentiality or privacy legislation in some form?- Jac

I received a letter from the liberals addressed to me directly over the weekend. There's no chance I've signed up for any communication from them — surely this is a breach of confidentiality or privacy legislation in some form?
- Jac
Hi Jac,
It's actually within the law.

A registered political party is exempt from the Privacy Act 1988, as is a political representative when carrying out an exempt political activity.A phone call, email or text message from a registered political party is also exempt from most spam and telemarketing rules.
A registered political party is exempt from the Privacy Act 1988, as is a political representative when carrying out an exempt political activity.
A phone call, email or text message from a registered political party is also exempt from most spam and telemarketing rules.
But how did they get your details? Well, the Australian Electoral Commission may have given them your address:
In line with the Commonwealth Electoral Act 1918, the AEC may provide the name, address and gender of electors to prescribed authorities.

No-one likes unsolicited mail, but political parties aren't breaking the law by sending them to you. You might just have to get in contact with the Liberal Party and ask them to take you off the mailing list.
Seats in focus: Point Cook
Point Cook was first contested at the 2022 election but is almost entirely made up of the abolished district of Altona, which was a Labor-held seat for its entire 30-year history.
Former attorney-general Jill Hennessy held Altona for 12 years on safe margins.

She decided not to contest the renamed seat in 2022 and the party preselected Mathew Hilakari, a local of Seaford on the other side of Port Phillip Bay and brother of Victorian Trades Hall Council secretary Luke Hilakari.
Labor's primary vote fell by nearly 10 percentage points in 2022, partly due to the crowded field of 15 candidates, including independent Joe Garra, who polled 7 per cent.
After preferences, the swing against Labor was 4.4 per cent.

Further swings against Labor in this seat could present an opportunity for a challenger, but it is unclear if any non-Labor candidate can consolidate enough support to overcome Point Cook's 8 per cent margin.
🎧: Does this election matter outside Victoria?
The Victorian state election is being regarded as something of a litmus test for Australian politics.
Polls suggest voters are turning away from the incumbent Labor Party in droves, and the Liberal-National Coalition is likely to pull off its first win in 12 years.
Minor parties One Nation and the Greens have seen huge growth in their support as voters turn away from the major parties.
Hear more from the ABC's Annie Brown on the Top Stories podcast:
The Coalition–One Nation connection
What evidence is the left basing their arguments on that Jess is teaming up with One Nation?- Concerned Voter
What evidence is the left basing their arguments on that Jess is teaming up with One Nation?
- Concerned Voter
Hello Concerned Voter,
Certainly the potential alliance between the Coalition and One Nation has been a key line of attack for the Labor government this election campaign.

They've splurged on AI ads showing Opposition Leader Jess Wilson and One Nation leader Warren Pickering together, and even dedicated an entire website to the idea, telling Victorians not to "risk it".
When interviewed on 774 ABC Melbourne last month, Wilson was evasive as to whether she would accept One Nation's support to form government.
"There are going to be many hypotheticals," she told Raf Epstein."We are running to form majority government, we are not thinking about anything else."
"There are going to be many hypotheticals," she told Raf Epstein.
"We are running to form majority government, we are not thinking about anything else."
For One Nation's part, Pickering has said the same thing, telling the ABC they are focused on winning a majority.
But Labor's claims aren't without merit, as the Liberal Party's preferences indicate on their how-to-vote cards.

In Wilson's own electorate of Kew, she is preferencing One Nation candidate David Laird fourth, well above independent Sophie Torney at seventh, Labor's David Sun at eighth and the Greens' Jackie Carter at ninth.
Deputy Premier Gabrielle Williams accused Wilson of not being honest about her allegiances today, and Labor have been using the Liberals' preferences as proof.
How are the parties tackling housing affordability?
There are more than 800,000 Victorians under the age of 30 eligible to vote in the 2026 state election.
While housing has not featured as a central issue during the campaign, many among the 17 per cent of the electorate who are gen Z identify housing affordability as a key priority.
Labor has committed to building more than 25,000 new homes in Melbourne and major regional cities, specifically for first-home buyers.
The Liberal-National Coalition is taking a different approach.
Instead of Labor's activity centres, it has promised to expand residential living around Melbourne's CBD by allowing more apartments to be built in places such as Fitzroy and Port Melbourne.
One Nation has said it will cut taxes and government fees that add to the cost of building new homes.
The Victorian Greens have proposed a rent freeze for two years across the state.
It has also advocated for $4 billion to be spent building and upgrading public housing and has vowed to abolish stamp duty for houses worth less than $1.1 million.

Seats in focus: Pascoe Vale
Prior to 2018, Pascoe Vale was a seat Labor could rely on, and it routinely won it with double-digit margins.

In 2014, the Labor primary vote slipped below 50 per cent for the first time since it was recreated ahead of the 1985 election, but this was easily chalked up as the consequence of losing a five-term incumbent in retiring MP Christine Campbell.
In 2018, however, Labor's primary vote fell by almost another 10 per cent, and its margin was pushed into the single digits by an independent candidate.
In 2022, the seat delivered the largest two-candidate preferred swing against Labor in the state, this time in favour of the Greens.
In 2026, Labor will be on high alert in a seat once considered its multicultural heartland. Like the neighbouring seat of Preston, Labor performs better in the north of the seat above Bell Street.
But Sydney Road also divides Pascoe Vale and the Greens perform better to the east.
In the partially overlapping federal seat of Wills at the 2025 election, the contest became even further polarised between the two parties.
Further complicating the contest is that almost 10 per cent of the primary vote went to socialist candidates at the last election and the Liberals preferenced the Greens.
Any change in these two factors could significantly shift the balance in this contest.
Another painful poll for Labor
The final polls before election day on Saturday are coming in.
The Age's Resolve Political Monitor this morning shows that Labor's primary vote in Victoria is just 20 per cent, well below the Coalition on 31 per cent.
Resolve found One Nation is outpolling Labor at 25 per cent and the Greens are polling at 13 per cent.
Earlier in the week, the Redbridge and Accent Research poll in the Australian Financial Review had the Coalition's primary vote at 33 per cent, One Nation on 23 per cent and Labor on 22 per cent.
The Greens were on 15 per cent.
Both polls showed Liberal leader Jess Wilson well ahead of Premier Ben Carroll and One Nation leader Warren Pickering as preferred leader.
Yet another 'pub test' failure
Carroll is then asked about separate reports in the Herald Sun that claim Victorian criminals are being ordered to stay at home and knit scarves as part of their community corrections orders.
Once again, the premier says he does not approve.

"That does not pass the pub test, and if I'm re-elected premier, I will see that that ceases," he says."You should be out doing rubbish on our freeways, you should be removing graffiti, and doing all those things that are a community corrections orders."
"That does not pass the pub test, and if I'm re-elected premier, I will see that that ceases," he says.
"You should be out doing rubbish on our freeways, you should be removing graffiti, and doing all those things that are a community corrections orders."
Carroll asked about reported $16.5 million delay

Premier Ben Carroll is asked about reports in The Age that Jacinta Allan cost taxpayers $16.5 million by delaying level crossing works to keep trains running on the Frankston Line before the 2022 election.
Carroll says he cannot justify it, and that it "didn't pass the pub test".
"I've made it very clear, as premier from day one, I take financial responsibility very, very seriously," he says.
He is then asked whether he knew about the $16.5 million expenditure, and he says he only learned about it today from media reports.

Deputy premier attacks Jess Wilson's 'mean' policies
Deputy Premier Gabrielle Williams is asked about Labor's poor polling, which shows women turning away from the party.
She admits Labor is fighting an uphill battle in this election.

"We're coming to this election campaign as the clear underdogs, there's no doubt about that," she says."Probably the most consequential election of my lifetime, and I'd argue probably the most consequential state election of anybody's lifetime."
"We're coming to this election campaign as the clear underdogs, there's no doubt about that," she says.
"Probably the most consequential election of my lifetime, and I'd argue probably the most consequential state election of anybody's lifetime."
Williams takes aim at the opposition leader, saying she was not being honest with her true allegiances.

"Jess Wilson is trying to convince her constituents in Kew that she's a moderate. She's not a moderate," Williams says."She's teamed up with One Nation and she's embarked upon a policy agenda that is populist and mean, and that's being kind."
"Jess Wilson is trying to convince her constituents in Kew that she's a moderate. She's not a moderate," Williams says.
"She's teamed up with One Nation and she's embarked upon a policy agenda that is populist and mean, and that's being kind."
Labor in Broadmeadows for first campaign stop of the morning
Premier Ben Carroll and his deputy Gabrielle Williams joined Broadmeadows MP Kathleen Matthews-Ward at DPV Health in Broadmeadows to talk up Labor's health pledges.
As he has said during much of the campaign, Carroll reiterates health care is on the ballot at the election.
The premier says only his party will provide free dental care through a $460 million package to operate 20 public clinics.
"We expect literally tens of thousands to take access to this," he says."There is [sic] waitlists everywhere, we know more and more people are wanting to have access to free dental."
"We expect literally tens of thousands to take access to this," he says.
"There is [sic] waitlists everywhere, we know more and more people are wanting to have access to free dental."
Carroll is pressed on how many patients the clinics will be able to see a year for dental appointments.
He repeats that it will benefit tens of thousands of people a year, and "hundreds of thousands over the life of the investment".
How will One Nation perform in the election?
One Nation had its best ever statewide result at an election in March this year, when 22.9 per cent of South Australians voted for the party founded by Pauline Hanson.

It's trying to improve on that result this week, and the party's rise is the main reason that whoever wins the looming Victorian election will likely win it with a record low primary vote in the state.
But how many seats in the Legislative Assembly will it win?

Labor publishes 'Jess Wilson's Health Calculator'
Not to be outdone in election stunts, Labor has posted a virtual calculator, entitled "Jess Wilson's Health Calculator".
Deputy Premier Gabrielle Williams demonstrated how it worked to reporters this morning, punching in equations.
The answers generated all related to Liberal-One Nation cuts to services.
For example, entering 2+2 returns an answer of $40 billion in cuts to the healthcare system.
Labor have made the calculator available on a dedicated site, telling voters "don't risk it" with a Coalition-One Nation government.
Key Event
Greens eye off seats as support for Labor evaporates
With Labor bracing for a serious hit to its primary vote, progressive voters are looking elsewhere. And the Victorian Greens hope to be the beneficiary.

The Greens are confident of retaining seats in Melbourne, Richmond and Brunswick, and winning back Northcote and Prahran (held by the Liberal Party). The minor party is also eyeing off Footscray and Pascoe Vale, and, to a lesser extent, Preston and Albert Park.
The vibe on pre-poll booths, candidates from multiple parties have said, is that the Greens could end up in the second position in some surprising seats, too.
"We could end up in the two-party preferred [count] in a whole host of seats that no-one thought possible," leader Ellen Sandell told the ABC.
Candidate Nina Crawley even thought she could top Labor in Ivanhoe, held by Labor frontbencher Anthony Carbines on a strong 12.8 per cent margin.
"I think it's entirely possible it's going to be a Liberal-Green contest here," Crawley said.
Labor expects to hold on in this seat. Carbines on Tuesday said he took nothing for granted and would work for every vote until 6pm on Saturday.
Labor had hopes of retaking Greens territory, and still believes it is in with a chance in Richmond.
Sandell conceded Greens seats would always be hard-fought contests. But the minor party believes it'll be the one making inroads.
In Footscray, Greens candidate Elena Pereyra said rusted-on Labor voters were taking her how-to-vote cards at early voting booths.
"People have been saying to us, 'we've been lifelong Labor voters, but definitely not this time'. And they're taking our how-to-vote card with gusto," Pereyra said.
Local MP Katie Hall disputed that the Labor brand was hurting her chances.
"You're down here between several pieces of beautiful infrastructure we've delivered," Hall said. "The Greens have never laid a brick."
Footscray is also being targeted by the Victorian Socialists, running a strong ground game, which could result in a drawn-out count.

Welcome to the blog
Good morning and welcome to our coverage of the Victorian state election campaign.
The major parties will be out campaigning today, with just three days to go before election day.
We'll bring you all the major moments from their campaign stops on the road, plus more analysis on the key seats in play on November 28.
